extraction.title: The Next Big Five Inventory (BFI-2): Developing and Assessing a Hierarchical Model with 15 Facets to Enhance Bandwidth, Fidelity, and Predictive Power
extraction.venue: Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 113, 117-143
extraction.document_type: Empirical journal article: three-study scale development and validation (measurement instrument)
extraction.coverage: Full text read: all 4,130 lines of the extracted text (printed pp. 1-79), covering front matter, abstract, introduction, Study 1, Study 2, Study 3, general discussion, limitations, conclusion, references, Tables 1-11, Figures 1-4 (captions and surrounding text only; figure graphics are not in the text file), appendix (60-item form) and scoring key. Paul's markup: no markup files were supplied for this PDF, so paul_markup is empty. Domain check: the paper contains no content on lobbying, social networks, path-finding, allocation, elections, persuasion or turnout, legislators, or text-as-data measurement. "Nomological network" is a construct-validity term (Cronbach and Meehl, 1955), not a social network. Lexical sourcing of items from trait adjectives and IPIP phrases (Study 1, Phase 2) is the only text-related element.
extraction.theory: Big Five trait structure (Extraversion, Agreeableness, Conscientiousness, Negative Emotionality, Open-Mindedness) with a hierarchical facet level. Bandwidth-fidelity tradeoff (Cronbach and Gleser, 1957; John, Hampson, and Goldberg, 1991): broad traits predict broadly, narrow facets predict specifically. Facets are chosen as factor-pure (anchor the domain) plus complementary (broaden it). Acquiescent responding is a response style that biases reliability, structure and validity unless items are content-balanced (Jackson and Messick, 1958).
extraction.research_question: Can a brief Big Five inventory be built with a robust hierarchical structure (three facets per domain), balanced true-keyed and false-keyed content to control acquiescence, and greater bandwidth, fidelity and predictive power than the original 44-item Big Five Inventory (BFI), while keeping the BFI's focus, clarity and brevity?
extraction.data: Study 1 (item development): N = 1,137 members of the Eugene-Springfield Community Sample (Oregon adults), age 18-89 (M = 49.64, SD = 13.02), 52.9% female; 641 completed the BFI; 1,131 completed at least one trait-adjective list (885 adjectives); 995 completed at least one IPIP list (2,552 IPIP items); 401 completed all 12 IPIP lists. Study 2 (scale construction): N = 1,000 adults from personalitylab.org (500 men, 500 women), age 18-77 (M = 29.25, SD = 12.17), 79% US residents; all rated a 110-item pool. Study 3 (validation): internet sample N = 1,000 personalitylab.org visitors (500 men, 500 women), age 18-74 (M = 28.73); student sample N = 470 psychology students at a large public university (146 men, 313 women, 11 unreported), age 16-49 (M = 21.68). Subsamples: 8-week retest n = 110; peer reports n = 184 (60% friends, 30% romantic partners); behavioral self-reports (Schwartz values, about two weeks later) n = 439; psychological well-being n = 179; other Big Five measures (Mini-Markers, BFAS, NEO PI-R, NEO-FFI) n = 438. Unit: individual respondent. Study period: not stated in the text. Note: the student sample is 470 in the text but 459 in the gender breakdown of Table 5.
extraction.method: Rational-empirical scale development in three studies. Study 1: three facets per domain chosen as one factor-pure facet plus two complementary facets (pp. 15-18); marker adjectives correlated against 885 adjectives, 2,552 IPIP items and 44 BFI items to find item content (pp. 18-19); preliminary pool of 110 items (44 original, 19 revised, 47 new) with at least three true-keyed and three false-keyed items per facet (p. 19). Study 2: rational review plus convergent and discriminant correlations with preliminary scales, and balanced keying, to select 60 items (four per facet, 15 facets, 5 domains of 12 items) (pp. 21-22); PCA with varimax rotation on the development sample, which the authors flag as possibly favorably biased (p. 22). Study 3 (independent samples): alpha and retest reliability; self-peer correlations; PCAs of raw and within-person-centered items; five-component varimax solutions for domains and facets with Tucker-type congruence; CFA of five model sets per domain (single domain, single domain plus acquiescence, positive/negative items, three facets, three facets plus acquiescence; acquiescence factor loadings fixed at 1 and uncorrelated with substantive factors); monotrait-heteromethod and heterotrait correlations with other Big Five measures; IRT test information comparisons with the BFI; and regressions predicting 20 self- and peer-reported criteria from BFI domains, post hoc BFI facets, BFI-2 domains and BFI-2 facets, with facets chosen by forward regression (inclusion p < .01, maximum three predictors) (pp. 22-38).
extraction.identification: None in the causal sense. This is an observational psychometric validation. Acquiescence is handled three ways: content-balanced keying (equal true- and false-keyed items per scale), within-person centering of items (p. 10, p. 30), and modeling acquiescence as a latent method factor in CFA (p. 32-33). Validity evidence is correlational (convergent, discriminant, self-peer, and criterion correlations and regressions). No causal or quasi-experimental design is used.
extraction.scope: Population: adults in economically developed English-speaking nations, mainly young or middle-aged and mostly with at least high-school education (Study 1 community sample from Oregon; Studies 2-3 volunteers from personalitylab.org, an online feedback site; Study 3 student sample from one public university). Not representative; the authors say population norms are still needed (p. 46). Era: not stated in the text. Institution: not applicable beyond the named samples. Measure scope: Big Five domains plus 15 facets, 60 items, 10 minutes or less.

key_findings.finding: Hierarchical model: 15 facets (three per Big Five domain) selected as one factor-pure plus two complementary facets per domain. Extraversion: Sociability, Assertiveness, Energy Level. Agreeableness: Compassion, Respectfulness, Trust. Conscientiousness: Organization, Productiveness, Responsibility. Negative Emotionality: Anxiety, Depression, Emotional Volatility. Open-Mindedness: Intellectual Curiosity, Creative Imagination, Aesthetic Sensitivity.
key_findings.location: Study 1, Phase 1, pp. 15-18; Table 1, p. 61; Conclusion of Study 1, p. 20
key_findings.numbers: 15 facets; 3 per domain; 110-item preliminary pool (44 original, 19 revised, 47 new)

key_findings.finding: Final BFI-2: 60 items, four per facet, 12 per domain. Reliability in the scale-development sample (Study 2): domain alphas .87 E, .83 A, .88 C, .91 N, .84 O; facet alphas .65-.84, mean .76. First PCA: all 15 facets loaded most strongly on their intended component (primary loadings at least .73, M = .80); all 60 items loaded most strongly on the intended component (at least .41, M = .60).
key_findings.numbers: 60 items; domain alpha .83-.91; facet alpha .65-.84 (M = .76); facet primary loadings >= .73 (M = .80); item primary loadings >= .41 (M = .60)

key_findings.finding: Study 3 reliability: all five domain alphas were at least .83 internet and .85 student; eight-week retest of domains was at least .76 (student). Facet alphas ranged .66-.85 in each sample (mean .76 internet, .77 student); facet retest .66-.83 (mean .73).
key_findings.location: Study 3, Reliability section, p. 28; Tables 2-3, pp. 62-63
key_findings.numbers: domain alpha >= .83 (internet), >= .85 (student); domain retest >= .76; facet alpha .66-.85; facet retest mean .73

key_findings.finding: Discrimination: absolute correlations among domains averaged .20 (internet) and .24 (student). Within-domain facet correlations averaged .53 (internet) and .55 (student), versus absolute between-domain facet correlations of .16 and .19.
key_findings.location: Study 3, pp. 28-29; Table 2, p. 62; Table 3, p. 63
key_findings.numbers: domain intercorrelation mean |r| = .20/.24; within-domain facet r = .53/.55; between-domain facet |r| = .16/.19

key_findings.finding: Self-peer agreement (student sample, peer n = 184): domain agreement .42-.69 (mean .56) versus absolute discriminant mean .11. Facet agreement .27-.73 (mean .49), within-domain discriminant mean .32, between-domain discriminant mean .10. Thirteen of 15 self-reported facets and 14 of 15 peer-reported facets had their strongest correlation with the corresponding facet on the other rater's side.
key_findings.numbers: domain agreement mean r = .56; facet agreement mean r = .49; 13/15 and 14/15 strongest-match counts

key_findings.finding: Acquiescence: PCA of 60 raw items gave six components above the scree line (Big Five plus an acquiescence component) in both samples. Within-person centering removed the extra component. Five varimax components of centered items reproduced the Big Five, with primary loadings averaging .62 (internet) and .61 (student); congruence with raw-item components was .97 or higher.
key_findings.location: Study 3, Domain-level structure, pp. 30-31; Figure 1, p. 73; Table 6, pp. 66-67
key_findings.numbers: raw-item PCA: 6 components vs 5 after centering; primary loadings M = .61 (internet raw), .60 (student raw), .62 (internet centered), .61 (student centered); congruence >= .97

key_findings.finding: Facet-level acquiescence: the PCA of 15 facet scales showed only five components above the scree line (first five eigenvalues 4.05, 2.16, 1.90, 1.60, 1.32 in the internet sample, then 0.56 or lower), so the content-balanced facets did not produce an acquiescence component. Facet primary loadings were at least .73 (M = .81, internet) and at least .67 (M = .79, student), with congruence .98 or higher.
key_findings.numbers: 5 components above scree; eigenvalues 4.05, 2.16, 1.90, 1.60, 1.32; facet primary loadings >= .73 (M = .81) and >= .67 (M = .79)

key_findings.finding: Confirmatory factor analysis within domains: a single-domain model fit poorly (CFI <= .805 internet, <= .800 student). Adding acquiescence or separating positive and negative items gave a large fit gain for Agreeableness but still poor fit (CFI <= .876 / .850). The three-facet model fit acceptably or nearly acceptably for E, C, N, O (CFI >= .902 / .895), and the three-facets-plus-acquiescence model fit acceptably for all domains (CFI >= .930 / .932).
key_findings.numbers: single-domain CFI <= .805 / .800; three facets CFI >= .902 (internet) / .895 (student) for E, C, N, O; three facets plus acquiescence CFI >= .930 / .932; RMSEA about .054-.075 for the best model per domain (Agreeableness .054 / .058)

key_findings.finding: Convergence with other Big Five measures (student sample): monotrait-heteromethod correlations averaged .92 with the original BFI, .82 with the BFAS, .80 with Mini-Markers, .75 with NEO-FFI and .72 with NEO PI-R; absolute heterotrait-heteromethod correlations averaged .21. Gains over the original BFI were largest for Agreeableness (.75 vs .70) and Open-Mindedness (.76 vs .72).
key_findings.numbers: convergent r: BFI .92, BFAS .82, Mini-Markers .80, NEO-FFI .75, NEO PI-R .72; heterotrait mean |r| = .21; A .75 vs .70; O .76 vs .72

key_findings.finding: Facet convergence: 53 BFI-2 facet correlations with same-domain BFAS aspects and NEO PI-R facets were at least .50, and each facet had a distinctive profile (for example, Assertiveness with BFAS Assertiveness r = .85; Organization with Order r = .74; Depression with Withdrawal r = .77).
key_findings.location: Study 3, Facet-level associations, pp. 35-36; Figure 3, pp. 74-76 (N = 438)
key_findings.numbers: 53 correlations >= .50; r = .85, .74, .77 as listed

key_findings.finding: Information: IRT test information was similar in shape for BFI and BFI-2 domains, but the BFI-2 gave about 55% more information on Negative Emotionality, 15% on Extraversion, 29% on Agreeableness, 12% on Open-Mindedness and 11% on Conscientiousness.

Predictive power: across 20 self- and peer-reported criteria, mean R-squared was .25 for BFI domains, .27 for post hoc BFI facets, .27 for BFI-2 domains and .33 for BFI-2 facets. Entering BFI-2 facets after BFI domains added significant variance for 14 of 20 criteria.
key_findings.location: Nomological network section, pp. 37-39; Table 11, p. 72; Figure 4, p. 77; footnote 7, pp. 38-39
key_findings.numbers: mean R2 = .25 (BFI domains), .27 (post hoc BFI facets), .27 (BFI-2 domains), .33 (BFI-2 facets); 14/20 criteria with significant incremental R2 for BFI-2 facets

key_findings.finding: Domain-level criterion patterns were nearly identical between BFI and BFI-2: column-vector correlations of zero-order correlations across 20 criteria averaged .98, as did standardized coefficients. Associations were slightly stronger for BFI-2 domains, giving higher explained variance.
key_findings.numbers: column-vector r = .98 (zero-order and standardized coefficients)

key_findings.finding: Facet-level predictors were distinct and conceptually meaningful. Examples (Table 10, r/beta): Benevolence predicted by Compassion (.47/.29) and Trust (.45/.28); Self-direction by Intellectual Curiosity (.44/.39); Stress resistance by Emotional Volatility (-.47/-.32) and Anxiety (-.46/-.28); Positive relations by Depression (-.53/-.38).
key_findings.numbers: see Table 10 r/beta values listed

key_findings.finding: Acquiescence index: averaging all 60 raw items without reversing false-keyed items gives a yea-saying or nay-saying index (range 1.00 to 5.00). The authors propose the BFI-2 for studying acquiescence itself.
key_findings.numbers: range 1.00-5.00 across 60 items

limitations: Samples are mostly young or middle-aged adults with at least high-school education; population norms are not yet available (p. 46). Reliability and validity among older adults and less-educated respondents are untested (pp. 46-47). The BFI-2's revisions for easier wording have not been directly tested for improved measurement among younger or less-educated respondents (p. 46).
All participants lived in economically developed English-speaking nations, so cross-cultural structure and correlates are untested (pp. 46-47).

Brevity forces exclusions. Domain-level: traits beyond the Big Five and constructs such as characteristic adaptations and narrative identity are excluded (p. 47). Facet-level: behavioral Open-Mindedness facets and peripheral facets such as excitement-seeking, modesty, deliberation and impulsivity are excluded (pp. 47-48). Item-level: anger/irritability content is measured only indirectly through Emotional Volatility (p. 48).

Study 2 facet and domain reliability and PCA results come from the same sample used to refine the item pool, so they may be favorably biased by capitalization on chance; the authors therefore emphasize Study 3 (p. 22).

Study 3 internet and student samples are self-selected (online feedback-seekers and course participants). The student sample is strongly gendered (313 women, 146 men) and the internet sample reports higher Open-Mindedness and Negative Emotionality than students (p. 29-30).

The 4-item facet scales have modest reliability (facet alphas .66-.85), and the authors note some Schwartz-value criteria have low alphas (.27-.70), which they retained as an a priori criterion set (p. 26-27).
Self-reported behavioral and psychological criteria come from single-method self-report, and peer reports are from a subsample of acquaintances (n = 184).

The authors recommend simple item aggregation for new studies. Regression-derived equations for switching from BFI to BFI-2 are available from the first author (footnote 3, p. 34), not reported in the text.

summary_md:
Soto and John build the BFI-2, a 60-item self-report Big Five inventory. It has 15 facets, three per domain, and each facet has four items with equal numbers of true-keyed and false-keyed items. Validation in independent internet (N = 1,000) and student (N = 470) samples gives domain alphas of at least .83 and facet alphas of .66 to .85. Self-peer agreement averages .56 at the domain level and .49 at the facet level (peer n = 184). Convergence with other Big Five instruments runs from .72 (NEO PI-R) to .92 (BFI). Raw-item PCA finds a sixth component, acquiescence. Within-person centering removes it, and the content-balanced facet scales never produce it. Across 20 self- and peer-reported criteria, BFI-2 facets explain more variance than domains (mean R2 .33 vs .27). The authors stress that facet quality matters more than the number of facets.

Nothing in the paper concerns legislators, lobbying or text. It bears on Paul's systems only through measurement mechanics. (1) The LLM item reader (big5_llm.py) says it uses "balanced keying", but the code keys O, C, E and A at 3 true to 1 false. Only ES is balanced. By the paper's acquiescence logic, a rater that tends to mark items +1 would push O, C, E and A up together and inflate their intercorrelation. The system already worries about this kind of halo. (2) The dormant expert-panel instrument is BFI-2-XS, which takes one item per BFI-2 facet. That panel was CANCELED (see flags). (3) The affective-N LLM read sums pessimism, anxiety, depression and volatility, which roughly match the BFI-2 Negative Emotionality facets. In the paper those facets predict different criteria. (4) The self-peer agreement figures give a realistic ceiling for reading convergence between text-based traits and gold ratings. All transfers are indirect: the paper studies general-population self-report, while the system reads politicians' text with LLM and lexical methods. Everything here is UNVERIFIED (DE-062).

bearings.paper_claim: PCA of the 60 raw items gave six components (Big Five plus acquiescence) in both samples. Within-person centering removed the sixth. The five centered components had primary loadings averaging .62 (internet) and .61 (student), with congruence .97 or higher. The 15 facet scales gave five components above the scree line (eigenvalues 4.05, 2.16, 1.90, 1.60, 1.32, then 0.56 or lower). Averaging raw unreversed items gives an acquiescence index from 1.00 to 5.00.
bearings.paper_location: Study 3 domain-level structure pp. 30-31 (Table 6, Table 7, Figure 1); General Discussion p. 45
bearings.system_side: big5_llm.py docstring line 7 says balanced keying. The ITEMS table has 3 true-keyed and 1 false-keyed item for O, C, E and A (negatives at lines 59, 63, 67, 71) and 2 and 2 for ES (lines 74-75). The keyed mean is at line 344. Under an all-yes response the four 3:1 traits score +0.5 and ES scores 0.
bearings.transfer_conditions: The acquiescence mechanism carries over only if the LLM shows a +1 tendency on observer items, which is untested. Under the paper's logic a yea-saying tendency lifts O, C, E and A together and leaves ES alone, so it would not create the A-ES correlation by itself. The paper's content balancing controls acquiescence at the scale level, not at the item level.
bearings.verifier_note: Paper numbers and page locations verified. The code keying and the docstring-versus-table mismatch are real. Not verified: the CT-CM MISS verdict and the A-ES halo of about .21 were not found in the repo files searched; big5_ctcm.py contains only the bar logic and branch text. The claim that content-balanced facets never produce acquiescence overstates the paper, which says they effectively control it in the facet PCA only (p. 31) and that acquiescence still biases same-domain facet associations (p. 33).

summary_issues: The sentence saying content-balanced facet scales never produce acquiescence overstates the paper. The paper says they effectively control it in the facet PCA (p. 31), but it also says acquiescence still biases same-domain facet associations (p. 33).
The convergence range of .72 to .92 comes from the student sample (N = 438, pp. 34-35); the summary leaves out that qualifier.
The expert panel sentence says the BFI-2-XS takes one item per BFI-2 facet. That fact comes from the companion short-form paper, not from this JPSP BFI-2 paper.

extraction.document_type: Journal article preprint (SSRN electronic copy, 41 pp.). Methods and metrics paper with grid examples, computer-generated Minnesota plans and Wisconsin litigation plans.
extraction.coverage: Read the full text file (2,501 lines, pp.1-41): abstract, introduction, related work, notation, Section 4 (county-split measures and grid examples, Table 1), Section 5 (least-change measures, grid examples, Table 2), Section 6 (Minnesota Table 3 and Wisconsin Table 4), conclusion, and all 57 references. Paul's markup: none. The Paul markup spec for this file was '(none)', and no annotation file for hash 76b06f81a37b exists in _annots. So paul_markup is empty.
extraction.research_question: How should 'preserve subdivisions' (county splitting) and 'least change from a prior district plan' be measured, and do different defensible measures rank the same maps differently, so that the criteria can be gamed by choosing a metric?
extraction.theory: No formal game-theoretic model. The conceptual frame is measurement dependence: a vague criterion admits many metrics, and each metric favors different plans. The paper uses information-theoretic measures (Shannon entropy, Variation of Information) and a pair-counting index (Fowlkes-Mallows) borrowed from clustering and information theory. It defines 'gameable' as 'exploitable or manipulable', not in the classic game-theoretic sense (p.2 fn.2).
extraction.data: Unit: district plans built from base units (precincts/VTDs, census blocks, wards). No voters are modeled. (1) Hand-built 24x24 grid example: 9 counties, four districts of 144 cells each, population 1 per cell; 7 plans scored on county-split metrics (Table 1, p.13). (2) 10x9 grid example: 84 precincts, 84 people, 90 land units, 4 districts of 21 people; baseline plus 4 balanced variants (Fig. 7 p.17; Table 2 p.27). (3) Minnesota: a 2012 congressional baseline, the 2022 court-ordered map, and 10 search-generated plans. Built from VTDs with up to 1% population deviation, using 2020 Census data (Table 3 p.29; Sec 6.1 p.27-28). (4) Wisconsin: 2012 baseline plus 6 congressional plans submitted in 2021 litigation (Governor, Hunter, Congressmen, Congressmen-alt, Mathematicians, PMC), scored at ward level after transferring block assignments (Table 4 p.35; fn.11 p.34). Period: 2012 baseline, 2020 Census, 2021 litigation, 2022 court map. Sample sizes: 7 grid plans, 4 change-grid variants, 11 Minnesota maps, 6 Wisconsin submissions.
extraction.method: Descriptive metric comparison (no inference). Section 4 defines county-split measures in four families: count-based (counties split, unnecessarily split, total county parts, split-county parts, unnecessary split-county parts, total county fragments), boundary-based (intra-county cut edges, and their length), entropy-based (Shannon entropy, Even Splits score, Square Root Entropy) and weighted variants. Section 5 defines least-change measures in matching-based form (People, Area, Precinct change), matching-free boundary forms (common-refinement perimeter, symmetric-length and symmetric-cut-edge perimeter), pairing forms (incumbent-people, incumbent-precinct, precinct-pair change), and Fowlkes-Mallows and Variation of Information. Each measure is computed on hand-built grid plans with worked arithmetic. Minnesota and Wisconsin plans are scored on all measures. Computer-generated Minnesota plans come from local search using ReCom and flip moves (DeFord-Duchin-Solomon 2021; Fifield et al. 2020), each run to maximize or minimize one metric. This search is not representative sampling. Plans 1-5 in Table 1 were hand-designed to illustrate properties, not produced by the optimizer (fn.4 p.12).
extraction.identification: None. The paper makes no causal or statistical identification claim. Its validity rests on the metrics being well defined and computed correctly. Verification is by hand-worked examples on the grids (e.g., Shannon ~1.821, Even Splits ~4.804 for Fig. 2; FM ~21%, VI ~22.8% for Fig. 7) and by the public replication repository.
extraction.scope: Population: US congressional and state-legislative district plans, with state examples from many states' constitutions and statutes (Iowa, Wyoming, Kentucky, South Carolina, Pennsylvania, Nebraska, Ohio, North Carolina, Washington, Idaho, Michigan, Louisiana, Kansas, New Mexico, New York, Utah). Empirical cases: Minnesota (2012 and 2022 congressional maps) and Wisconsin (2021 litigation). Institution: state courts and special masters in redistricting impasses (e.g., Wisconsin Supreme Court, New Hampshire Supreme Court, Minnesota Special Redistricting Panel). Era: the 2010-2022 cycle. Only three states have district-core preservation in constitution or statute (NM, NY, UT, per Yablon, cited at p.15). The paper itself describes the Wisconsin ruling as one of the 'most notorious' least-change decisions (p.15).

key_findings.finding: Different county-split metrics pick different best plans on the same grid set. Plan 2 has the fewest counties split (1), Plan 3 has the lowest Shannon entropy (1.265) and fewest intra-county cut edges (18), and Plan 4 has the lowest Even Splits score (2.485) and fewest total county fragments (11).

key_findings.finding: The most compact grid plan (Plan 6, designed to maximize compactness) splits the most counties apart from Plan 7. The paper says plans designed to preserve counties do better across the board.
key_findings.numbers: Plan 6: 48 cut edges (lowest), 5 counties split, 16 total county parts. Plan 7: 154 cut edges, 9 counties split.

key_findings.finding: Worked sample plan (Fig. 2, 24x24 grid, 4 districts of 144): splits 3 counties (C2, C5, C7); 12 total county parts; 14 total county fragments; 34 intra-county cut edges; Shannon entropy about 1.821; Even Splits about 4.804.
key_findings.numbers: 3 counties split; 12 parts; 14 fragments; 34 intra-county cut edges; Shannon 1.821; Even Splits 4.804.

key_findings.finding: Change metrics pull apart. On the grid balanced variants, Plan 2 ties Plan 3 for best People Change (9.5%), while Plan 1 has the best Area Change (7.8%). The text says Plan 2 has the second-worst Area Change.

Minnesota: the court-ordered 2022 map is not the best on any measure but is 'far from the worst'. Plans 7-10 were built to do well on change measures, and the best change scores are spread across four plans.
key_findings.numbers: Court-ordered: 9 counties split, 99 total county parts, Shannon 7.84, People change 7.50%, Area change 13.07%. Best change scores: Plan 8 People 1.93%, Plan 7 Precinct 1.09%, Plan 10 Area 0.28%.

key_findings.finding: Population-based and incumbency-based change can diverge sharply. Plan 8 and Plan 9 move almost the same share of people, but Plan 9's incumbent-people change is far worse because an incumbent's precinct moved. The text says Plan 9 moves 0.03% more people than Plan 8; Table 3 shows the reverse (1.90% vs 1.93%), so this is an internal inconsistency to verify.

key_findings.finding: Trade-off between county splits and least change in the Minnesota set: no plan is best on both families. Plans 1 and 2 have some of the best county-split scores and some of the worst least-change scores.
key_findings.numbers: Plan 1: 1 county split, 0 unnecessarily split; People change 86.30%. Plan 2: 2 counties split, People change 98.07%.

key_findings.finding: Wisconsin real-world plans: the Mathematicians plan is best on nearly all county-split metrics. Congressmen-alt is best on several change metrics but worst on every county-split metric. The court adopted the Governor's plan. No submitted map is best on both families.

key_findings.finding: Wisconsin least-change was undefined in the November 2021 ruling (the court 'called for a least-change approach'). The later final order defined it as the number of voters who remained in their old districts. This gave multiple parties grounds to claim their maps changed least.

key_findings.finding: Conclusion: vague criteria are gameable. The paper recommends that states define metrics explicitly but avoid hard numeric thresholds (e.g., a 2-county maximum), because feasibility depends on political geography.

limitations: Relaxed constraints for tractability: plans built from precincts/VTDs/wards rather than census blocks, and population deviation up to 1%, whereas congressional plans need one-person balance (Conclusion p.37; Sec. 6.1 p.28).

The Minnesota court-ordered map was coarsened to precincts, which introduced a 1.3% population deviation not reflective of the actual districts. The sample maps are not valid proposals under one-person, one-vote (fn.9 p.28).
Wisconsin metrics were computed at ward level, so figures would differ slightly at the block level (fn.11 p.34).
Grid plans 1-5 and 6-7 were hand-designed to illustrate properties, not optimizer output (fn.4 p.12).
Incumbent-based metrics ignore whether incumbents are seeking reelection (p.22).
The measures surveyed are not exhaustive (p.25). Population-based and area-based scores are sensitive to projection (p.18), and the entropy measures use population only.
Stated future work: communities of interest, compactness and partisan fairness are not analyzed (p.37).
Internal inconsistency to verify: text (p.33) says Plan 9 moves 0.03% more people than Plan 8, but Table 3 (p.29) gives 1.90% vs 1.93%.
measures: County-split: number of counties split; number of counties unnecessarily split; total county parts; split-county parts; unnecessary split-county parts; total county fragments; intra-county cut edges (count and length); Shannon entropy; Even Splits score; Square Root Entropy.

summary_md:
Becker and Gold take two common redistricting criteria, preserving counties and changing the prior plan as little as possible, and show that each can be measured in many defensible ways. The measures disagree about which map is best. On a hand-built 24x24 grid, Plan 2 splits the fewest counties (1), Plan 3 has the lowest Shannon split entropy (1.265) and Plan 4 has the best Even Splits score (2.485). In a 10x9 grid example, the plan that ties for the lowest People Change (9.5%) has the second-worst Area Change (13.3% against a best of 7.8%). On Minnesota (11 maps) and Wisconsin (6 litigation maps), no map is best on both a county-split measure and a least-change measure. Two Minnesota plans move almost the same share of people (1.90% and 1.93%), yet their incumbent-people change is 13.90% against 1.93%. The paper's verdict is that a vague criterion lets each party pick the metric its own map wins on. Its recommendation is to define metrics explicitly but avoid hard numeric caps. The analysis is descriptive only, with no inference. It used relaxed population balance (up to 1%) and precinct or ward units, and the study was funded by Jenner & Block.

The paper has no bearing on the influence engine, stance, SNA or Mentat. Its relevance is narrow: the system's district-geography plumbing. That code compares old and new congressional boundaries (CD116 vs CD119 in `redistricting_density.py`, and the CBP/ACS vintage mismatch in the census scraper) and orients Cook PVI across the mid-decade redistricting. In both places the system uses single, implicit change measures: whether the seat label changed, a weighting based on block counts, and a state-list flag plus a PVI-shift flag. The paper shows that this kind of choice decides the answer. Its weaker, general lesson, that choosing a metric reorders the winners, also applies to the score blend's three weight sets, which are unratified and documented inconsistently. Everything in this note is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it (DE-062).

The county-split measures in Table 1 disagree on the best plan (fewest counties split is Plan 2 with 1; lowest Shannon entropy is Plan 3 at 1.265; lowest Even Splits is Plan 4 at 2.485).

paul_alignment: Paul has no annotations on this paper, and none of his component positions cites redistricting-metric literature, so there is no takeaway to agree with or go stale. Two points connect to positions he does hold. First, Paul endorses Cook PVI as a vulnerability measure (Gaynor). This paper adds the caveat that once maps are redrawn, which PVI belongs to which member depends on how district change is measured, and the system currently handles that with flags and his D-107 overrides rather than a change metric. Second, the paper's general warning that metric choice is gameable fits his position that the blend weights are owner policy with no literature behind them. It argues for documenting one weight set rather than for any particular weights.

related.why: Both evaluate redistricting plans. Best et al. ask whether commissions avoid partisan gerrymanders; Becker and Gold show that procedural criteria such as county splits and least change can be gamed through metric choice. Item file title confirmed.

Both concern congressional district geography at block or precinct level. DeLuca and Curiel validate Bayesian surname-and-geocoding inference for congressional redistricting; the link is measurement validity for district-level inputs, not change metrics.

A 2024 Cook Political Report ratings piece in the same input family as the Cook district PVI that drives COMPET_MULT. The link is conceptual only: Becker and Gold measures say how far a district moved, which governs whether a PVI value carries over. Report content was not checked here.

summary_md:
Chohan's discussion paper is an essay, not an empirical study. It describes Fairshake, the crypto super PAC network that also includes Protect Progress and Defend American Jobs, and argues that the industry has moved from crypto-anarchism through statism to an 'oligarchic' stage, using a Marxian stage model. Its numbers come from the press or from Fairshake itself: $203M raised for the 2024 cycle (p. 7), 253 supported candidates with no win rate and no counterfactual (p. 8), $78M already raised toward 2026 (p. 9), and an unsourced count of 100,000 crypto millionaires (p. 14). It names targeted races: Moreno over Brown in Ohio, against Tester in Montana, against Porter in a primary and against Bowman. It says these show 'decisive' influence (pp. 9-10) but estimates nothing, and it notes that many of the ads never mentioned crypto (p. 8).

For Paul's systems the paper adds no measurement or method. Its value is descriptive, and it points the same way in three places.

1. **Crypto money flows mostly through super PACs.** It is corporate-treasury money aimed at elections and often spent against candidates, not PAC contributions to candidate committees. That fits Mentat keeping a separate Super PAC channel and a support/oppose field. It also shows that Melange's flip model cannot see this money at all, because its industry money term counts only direct bank and finserv PAC receipts.
2. **The series breaks in 2024.** A new entrant spent at record scale in its first big cycle, which supports the registry decision to decline a crypto forecast for now.
3. **Primary-contest plays exist in practice.** Industry money has been used to contest primaries, the same kind of play the electoral-plays module models.

None of the paper's claims about effects on outcomes can be used as evidence. That applies especially to the competitiveness multiplier, where reciprocity is still not validated.

gaps_exposed: Melange's flip and money-response models do not include super PAC independent expenditures. They see only direct PAC contributions to members ('banks' and 'finserv'). For an industry like crypto that spends mainly as outside money, competitor pressure is invisible to the engine.

The model has no deterrence or spillover term. In the paper's account, punishing a visible opponent such as Brown or Tester is a signal to other members. The engine's money terms act only on the member who receives the money.
Mentat keeps the attributed beneficiary estimate unbuilt, so crypto corporate-treasury money routed through super PACs cannot yet be tied to candidate-level support or oppose totals.
Crypto stays declined in the forecast registry. A cycle-phase method has no way to handle a new entrant whose first big cycle is a level break.

Every dollar figure is press-reported or self-reported ($203M, $78M) or unsourced (100,000 millionaires). Any reuse must name the source and the window (2024 cycle; 2026 to date as of about Jan 2025) and treat the figures as unverified against FEC.
The paper's 'oligarchy' and influence framing is normative. Do not carry that language onto staffer or revolving-door edges or into graph ranks (D-025).

It sits closest to his margin note on Kim J. 2025, 'I may need to take into account the presence of conflicting industries', and to his wish to map rival-industry champions. But it shows that actor working through super PAC spending rather than lobbying filings or bill positions, which is a channel his conflicting-industries idea and the Melange money engine do not yet model. The paper is also the kind of confident ROI and influence narrative that Paul's own evidence tests (the sector-growth study, the competitiveness lane) have not borne out, so it should not raise his confidence in money effects.

extraction.research_question: Can the Big Five personality traits of a Twitter user be predicted automatically from their tweets using NLP, sentiment analysis and machine learning/regression, as a scalable alternative to questionnaire-based assessment? (Abstract; Section 1.) The text never states a formal hypothesis.
extraction.theory: Big Five trait model, which the paper labels as "Creativity, Dependability, Sociability, Kindness, and Anxiety" (Sections 1-2, 3.3). These labels are non-standard: the conventional Big Five are Openness, Conscientiousness, Extraversion, Agreeableness and Neuroticism. Section 2 itself refers to "agreeableness and neuroticism", so the labelling is internally inconsistent. The paper also draws on the claim that linguistic cues and sentiment link to personality traits (Section 2), citing a Facebook meta-analysis at "[14]".
extraction.data: The paper describes a planned data pipeline, not an analysed dataset. Tweets are collected via the Twitter API using keywords, hashtags and user handles; fields include tweet text, user info, timestamps and interactions (Section 3.1). The system takes a Twitter handle and a user-specified number of tweets (Section 1). Unit: presumably one user's tweet set. Sample size (N): not reported. Time period: not reported. Source of trait labels for training: not stated ("Tweets are labelled according to personality traits using models like the Big Five", Section 3.3). No dataset name, size or download source is given.
extraction.method: Pipeline (Sections 3.1-3.6): (1) cleaning, removing URLs, mentions, hashtags, lowercasing and stopword removal; (2) tokenization; (3) TF-IDF vectorization, plus LIWC and other psycholinguistic features; (4) user profile features (follower count, tweet frequency, bio); (5) sentiment analysis of positive and negative tone; (6) classifiers named as Random Forest, Neural Networks and SVM (Section 3.3), and elsewhere Naive Bayes, SVM, RNN or BERT (Section 3.5 text), with supervised regression to output a percentage per Big Five trait (Sections 1, 3.5, Figure 5). Training uses cross-validation to limit overfitting. Evaluation uses accuracy, precision, recall and confusion matrices (Section 3.4). Feature importance is analysed (Section 3.5). The results are visualised as pie charts (Abstract; Section 4). Regression is described only in words and in Figure 5 (caption only). The paper contains no equations beyond the TF-IDF formula caption (Figure 2).
extraction.identification: None. The paper is a predictive pipeline with cross-validation. It makes no causal, quasi-experimental or instrumental claim, and no identification strategy is stated.
extraction.scope: Population: Twitter users generally, with English-language tokenization implied (Section 3.2 discusses English word boundaries). No demographic, country or language restriction is stated. Institution: a student engineering project at MIET College, Meerut (CSE department). Era: not stated. The paper's references run to 2024, so the work is presumably from around 2024-2025. Generalisability: not discussed beyond cultural-context future work.

summary_md:
**What the paper is.** This is a short SSRN proposal from a student engineering group at MIET College, Meerut. It describes a pipeline that would take a Twitter handle, clean and tokenize the tweets, and build TF-IDF, LIWC-style, sentiment and profile features (follower count, tweet frequency, bio). A classifier or regression would then output each Big Five trait as a percentage, shown in a pie chart. The paper reports no sample size, no data period, no source for its trait labels, and no accuracy figures. The model list changes between sections. The trait names are non-standard ("Creativity, Dependability, Sociability, Kindness, Anxiety"), and several citations do not match the reference list. The abstract's claim about stress detection has no method behind it. In short, this is a design sketch, not evidence.

**Why it matters here, and how little.** The only component it touches is Melange's lexical Big Five reader. That reader already does more than the paper proposes: LIWC-analog rates, Mairesse SMOreg weights, a refit to RKH targets, token-based low-confidence shrinkage, and reported held-out CV (mean .350 across the five traits, window and N as recorded in the brain). The project's validation record goes further still. The pre-registered nomological look rated lexical Big Five as unfit for behavioural prediction, and receptivity now runs on a behavioural basis. The paper offers nothing that could test or recalibrate any of this, and none of its features should be adopted on its authority. Two cautions transfer. First, its profile features (follower count, tweet frequency) are volume proxies of the kind the system has already rejected. Second, it outputs absolute "percentages" with no reference norm, while the system deliberately reports traits as z-scores relative to its own corpus. Read it as a negative example of an unvalidated trait-from-text claim, not as support.

bearings.paper_claim: Proposes predicting Big Five trait percentages from tweets with TF-IDF, LIWC/psycholinguistic categories, sentiment and profile features, using RF/SVM/NN (Sec 3.3) or NB/SVM/RNN/BERT (Sec 3.5) plus regression. No N, no label source and no accuracy, precision or recall values are reported. It says cross-validation and confusion matrices are used (Sec 3.4) but shows none.
bearings.system_side: A closed-vocabulary LIWC-analog reader (rates per 1000 words, with low-confidence flags below 1,500 tokens), weighted by Mairesse SMOreg and refit to RKH targets. Traits are z-scored relative to this corpus only. Held-out CV against RKH: E .510, A .406, C .363, ES .258, O .214. The system already implements, and has measured, the feature family the paper only proposes.
bearings.transfer_conditions: It does not transfer as evidence. There are no labels, no sample, no results, and the genre (general Twitter users) differs from legislators' floor speech and interviews. At most it is a list of candidate features. Its absolute 'percentage' outputs conflict with the system's rule that scores are meaningful only within this corpus. extraction.title: The strategic advantages of micro-targeted campaigning: A proof of principle Bayesian Agent-Based Model
extraction.year: 2017 per the metadata hint; the text itself shows no year (its latest cited work is Madsen 2016)
extraction.venue: Not stated in the text. Page numbers run 2651 to 2656, which suggests a proceedings or journal volume, but no venue name appears.
extraction.document_type: Peer-reviewed academic paper (simulation study with an agent-based model). The text does not label the article type.
extraction.coverage: Full text read in two chunks (lines 1 to 694 of the extracted text, about 34,400 characters), including abstract, introduction, model, simulation design, results, discussion and references. Paul's markup: none found. No annotation or sidecar file matching ID ef4355b0bd91 exists in _annots, annotations or _work under C:\Users\pgoff\Documents\research.
extraction.research_question: Does a micro-targeted campaign (MTC), which contacts only voters with a favourable view of the candidate's credibility, persuade the electorate more efficiently than a stochastic campaign that contacts voters at random? Can an agent-based model with a Bayesian source-credibility belief-updating rule simulate persuasion campaign strategies? The paper frames itself as an exploratory proof of concept.
extraction.theory: Bayesian source-credibility model (Harris et al., 2015; Bovens & Hartmann, 2003; Hahn et al., 2009/2012). Credibility is split into expertise (E, capability to give accurate information) and trustworthiness (T, willingness to give accurate information). The two are treated as orthogonal. Beliefs are revised with an expanded Bayes rule, p(h|rep), using conditional probabilities from Table 1 taken from Madsen (2016), so belief revision has no free parameters. Political campaign theory: the persuasion phase of a campaign is modelled separately from get-out-the-vote (Green & Gerber, 2008). Micro-targeting background draws on Issenberg (2012) and O'Neil (2016).
extraction.data: No empirical data. The study is a simulation. Units are simulated voters (agents). N = 10,000 voters per simulation, 2 candidates, 1 binary proposition (H = 0 or 1), 50 ticks (campaign days). Voter expertise and trustworthiness scores are drawn from normal distributions with mean 0.5 or 0.6 and SD 0.25. Voter prior belief is drawn from normal (mean 0.5, SD 0.25), bounded 0.01 to 1. The MTC candidate's reach is fixed at 20 contacts per tick. The non-MTC reach ratio runs from 1 to 10. The text does not report the number of replications or random seeds. The conditional probability table (Table 1) is garbled in the extraction, with values 80.38, 58.21, 34.63, 18.04, 22.59, 42.3, 59.90, 71.26 and no clear units.
extraction.method: Agent-based model (ABM) with two agent types, voters and persuaders. Persuaders are either MTC or stochastic (non-MTC). Voters are randomly distributed, with no spatial role, and have no links to each other. Persuaders make direct contacts. The non-MTC candidate contacts voters at random and states p(candidate) = 1. The MTC candidate contacts only voters whose signal factor (mean of T and E) exceeds 0.5, sampling randomly among eligible voters up to its reach, and states p(candidate) = 0. Each contacted voter replaces its belief with the posterior P(candidate|rep). A voter is contacted at most once per tick. At the end, each voter votes for the candidate it favours (p > 0.5). Design: 2 x 2 manipulation of mean credibility (0.5 or 0.6) crossed with non-MTC reach ratio 1 to 10. Outcome is the share of voters supporting the non-MTC candidate. Results are presented as a single figure (Fig. 2). No statistical tests, confidence intervals or sensitivity analysis are reported.
extraction.identification: None in the causal-inference sense. The mechanism is built in by design: the MTC selection rule and the Bayesian update are fixed, and the two manipulated inputs are credibility mean and reach ratio. The authors frame the study as a proof of concept and do not claim identification of real-world effects.
extraction.scope: Population: a simulated electorate of 10,000 homogeneous-process voters. Institution: a stylised two-candidate, single-proposition election with a persuasion phase only. Turnout is not modelled, since all voters vote with probability 1 at the end. Era: not stated. The model is motivated by contemporary micro-targeting in US-style campaigns, citing Issenberg (2012) and O'Neil (2016). The model does not include negative campaigning, multiple issues, voter networks or personality differences.

key_findings.finding: Under the Bayesian source-credibility rule, an MTC with the same reach consistently beats a stochastic campaign.
key_findings.numbers: MTC reach fixed at 20 per tick; non-MTC reach ratio 1 to 10 (ratio 1 = equal reach). Exact vote shares are only in Fig. 2 and are not given in the text.

key_findings.finding: With mean credibility 0.5, a stochastic (non-MTC) campaign is inefficient. Opinions are equally split, so blind contacts reach supporters and opponents in equal numbers. Blind campaigns only work when the candidate's average perceived credibility is above 0.5. Below that, they can be ineffective or harmful.
key_findings.numbers: Mean credibility 0.5 versus 0.6 (SD 0.25).

key_findings.finding: A non-MTC campaign with roughly double the reach cancels out the MTC advantage.
key_findings.numbers: Break-even at non-MTC reach about 2x the MTC reach (MTC reach = 20).

key_findings.finding: If the non-MTC reach ratio exceeds 2 and the non-MTC candidate's perceived credibility is above 0.5, the stochastic campaign beats the strategic one.
key_findings.numbers: Reach ratio > 2; credibility mean > 0.5.

key_findings.finding: Discussion restates that the MTC advantage is not general: a positively perceived stochastic candidate with greater reach can beat a strategic one.
key_findings.numbers: Non-MTC needs double reach to cancel the advantage.

key_findings.finding: The authors predict, without testing, that MTC efficiency rises with available voter data and with electorate complexity (belief systems, individual differences, voter-to-voter interaction). MTC costs are also predicted to rise with complexity.
key_findings.numbers: None reported; this is a prediction only.

limitations: The authors call the study exploratory. The model is 'necessarily simplified' and a 'proof of concept' (p. 2651, p. 2655).
Voters are cognitively homogeneous, with the same belief-revision process. There are no moral foundations, personality or reasoning-strategy differences (p. 2655).
Voters consider a single proposition, while real elections involve many issues, preferences and candidates (p. 2655).
The MTC segments only on candidate favourability, not on swing/secure status, policy preference or turnout likelihood (p. 2655).
Voters cannot communicate or influence one another. Social networks, community leaders and social nodes are absent, though the authors suspect MTCs would do better with them (p. 2653, p. 2655).
Real campaigners do not get a perfect signal from each voter. Noise was added to the voter signal, but the amount and form of that noise are not described in the text (p. 2655).
Turnout is not modelled. All voters vote with probability 1 at the end (p. 2652).
The conditional probabilities are taken from Madsen (2016) and not calibrated to this electorate (p. 2653).
No replications, confidence intervals, statistical tests or sensitivity analysis are reported. Results rest on one figure (Fig. 2).
Negative campaigning is not implemented (footnote 3, p. 2654), and the model is not tested against real campaign data.
Footnote 2 and the Table 1 layout are garbled in the extracted text, so the conditional-probability values cannot be checked against the printed table with confidence.
measures: Share of voters who favour the non-MTC candidate at end of campaign (y-axis of Fig. 2).
Non-MTC reach ratio, non-MTC reach divided by MTC reach (x-axis; 1 to 10).
Mean perceived credibility of each candidate (0.5 or 0.6), with SD 0.25 for the trustworthiness and expertise draws.
Voter signal factor: the mean of trustworthiness and expertise, with threshold 0.5 for MTC contact.
Voter prior belief p(candidate), drawn from normal (mean 0.5, SD 0.25), bounded 0.01 to 1.
Posterior belief P(candidate|rep) after each contact, from the Bayesian source-credibility formula with Table 1 conditionals.

summary_md:
Madsen and Pilditch build a small agent-based model as a proof of concept. Two candidates compete over 50 ticks for 10,000 simulated voters who are not connected to each other. Each contacted voter replaces its belief with a Bayesian source-credibility posterior. Credibility is split into expertise and trustworthiness, and the conditional probabilities come from Madsen (2016) with no free parameters. The micro-targeted campaign contacts only voters whose mean credibility score for it is above 0.5, 20 per tick. The stochastic campaign contacts voters at random, with reach set to 1 to 10 times the targeted campaign's.

Results:
- At equal reach, targeting wins.
- When mean credibility is 0.5, random contact is wasted, because contacts land on favourable and unfavourable voters in equal numbers.
- A random campaign with about twice the reach cancels the targeting advantage.
- Above a 2x reach ratio, and with credibility above 0.5, the random campaign wins.

All results come from one figure. The paper reports no replications, no intervals and no sensitivity analysis, and it does not model turnout, multiple issues, or voter-to-voter networks.

For Paul's systems this is weak evidence about mechanism, not a calibration source. It agrees with two design choices: contacts go only to receptive targets, and money is never spent trying to convert opponents. Both match the paper's finding that blind contact with low-credibility audiences is inefficient or harmful. It also says the advantage of targeting depends on reach, which no part of the system models. The closest analogue is Terrier's untapped-potential score for door canvassing. That score gives persuasion weight to undecided likely voters but carries no credibility or receptivity term for the messenger. That missing term is the variable that decides the paper's result. The paper does not touch the cosponsorship network, LDA, reciprocity, or the rank pillars. It gives no reason to change a constant. Every number it reports is a simulation output, not an estimate.

bearings.paper_claim: Persuasion contact with voters who give the messenger credibility at or below 0.5 is inefficient or harmful. Targeting only receptive voters (signal factor above 0.5) beats random contact at equal reach; random contact needs about 2x the reach to break even. Simulation only: N=10,000 agents, 50 ticks, targeted reach 20 per tick.
bearings.system_side: potential = (wp x (1-|2s-1|) x t + (1-wp) x s x (1-t)) x (1 + wi x i). The persuasion weight peaks for undecided likely voters (s = 0.5). The formula has no term for how credible the canvasser or candidate is to the person being contacted, and no term for backfire.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Partial transfer. Both concern voter-level persuasion targeting in a two-candidate race. The paper, however, uses unconnected simulated agents, a single proposition and no turnout, and its credibility values are drawn from distributions, not measured. It supports adding a messenger-credibility or backfire guard as a hypothesis to test against canvass results. It does not support any particular weight. Strength is weak because these are uncalibrated ABM outputs with no replications reported.

bearings.paper_claim: Under Bayesian source-credibility updating, contacts restricted to receptive targets (credibility signal above 0.5) convert better than untargeted contacts. Contacting audiences who view the source unfavourably moves them away from the source's position.
bearings.system_side: gate(n) = max(0.15, seed_prob x SGATE[tier]). SGATE falls from 1.00 for Highly Persuadable to 0.35 for Opponent, so the system already expects contacts with unreceptive targets to convert at lower rates. The model has no negative (backfire) outcome for a contact.
bearings.transfer_conditions: Directional agreement only. The paper's agents are voters, not legislators. Its unit is a source-credibility belief update, not a take-up decision about cosponsoring, and it estimates no take-up rates. The SGATE values remain unestimated design constants; this paper does not calibrate them.
bearings.component_link: [[systems/melange-influence-engine#Contingent seed activation gate|Contingent seed activation gate]]

bearings.paper_claim: Contact spent on audiences with an unfavourable view of the source is wasted or counterproductive. The targeted campaign's advantage comes entirely from never contacting those voters.
bearings.system_side: Members whose overall tier is Skeptic, Highly Skeptical or Opponent receive zero money in every allocator, which funds allies instead of trying to convert opponents. The gate fails open for members with no matrix row.
bearings.transfer_conditions: An analogy only. Campaign contacts with voters are not PAC dollars to legislators, and the paper has no money mechanism. It agrees with Paul's Furnas reading ('cultivate champions') but adds no new evidence about legislator behaviour.

gaps_exposed: Terrier's untapped potential has no messenger-credibility or backfire term. In the paper, the share of the audience that views the source favourably is the variable that decides whether contact helps or hurts.

No component models the trade-off between reach and targeting: how much more random reach makes up for targeting precision (the paper's break-even is about 2x). The allocators and turf planner treat contact capacity as a fixed budget, not a strategy choice.
None of the influence-engine contact models (SGATE, PERS) has a negative outcome for a contact. A contact with an Opponent only converts with low probability; it never pushes the member further away.
flags: The paper's results are simulation outputs from a single figure, with no replications, intervals or sensitivity analysis reported. None of its numbers (the 0.5 credibility threshold, the 2x break-even reach) should be quoted as empirical estimates or used to set SGATE, PERS or Terrier weights. If cited, it should be labelled as a theoretical proof of concept.
Per DE-062, this agent analysis is UNVERIFIED until a second path reproduces it.

The paper does not argue for either SNA proposal this project has rejected (dropping regular cosponsorship edges; per-edge volume normalization). It has no network at all, so there is nothing to flag there.
paul_alignment: Paul has not annotated this paper. It agrees with his Furnas-based position that ideological money cultivates champions rather than recruiting them, and with his seeding view taken from Chen et al. (contingency-aware seeding: legislators may or may not move when approached). Both are already built as the stance money gate and SGATE. His Broockman & Kalla and Kalla & Broockman highlights on the door canvass are about how the message is delivered. This paper adds a different dimension: who the messenger is to the voter. Terrier's potential formula encodes neither. Nothing in his notes is out of date relative to this paper.

related.why: Tappin measures persuasive returns to microtargeting with experiments; Madsen and Pilditch only simulate them. Tappin is the empirical check on this paper's claim that targeting has an advantage.
Simchon also studies the persuasive effects of political microtargeting, with generative-AI messages. It offers the empirical evidence this paper does not have.
Field evidence on persuasion from door canvassing, the real-world setting behind Terrier's untapped-potential score, which this paper treats only abstractly.
Both make contact conditional on the target's receptivity. Chen does it as contingency-aware seeding, which the system implements as SGATE; this paper does it as credibility-gated contact.
A two-candidate competitive voter-dynamics model on networks. It adds the voter-to-voter interaction this paper leaves out and says targeting would benefit from.

backlinks.why: An agent-based model of micro-targeted campaigning. Issue-specific, voter-position-dependent responses of the kind measured here are the empirical input such a model would need.

Both build agent-based simulation models of a political process (micro-targeted campaigning in Madsen; knowledge brokering in state agencies here), so they are the vault's two ABM references for any future agent-level extension of the influence engine.
Item file title matches Madsen and Pilditch 2017, an agent-based proof of principle for micro-targeted campaigning; this paper supplies the field-experimental counterpart with net-of-cost numbers.
